1.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Twelve cubic metres of air per person, give or take the racks. I keep doing the arithmetic and getting a number that sounds generous and feels small.

Seeded the first trays before dinner. Nothing to report and nothing to see — germination is four days out — but there is a difference between a habitat with seeds in it and one without, and I wanted us on the right side of that on the first night.
1.HEALTH OFFICER:
Baseline readings on all three of us before the hatch closed: weight, resting pulse, grip, sleep debt carried in from the week of preparation. Everyone arrived tired. That is normal and it is also a starting position I would rather not have.

Fourteen hours in. I have already learned that the floor by the water rack is the coldest place to stand, which matters more than it sounds — cold feet at the end of a shift is how people stop wanting to do the last task properly.

2.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
Forty-one messages today. I read all of them, twice, because reading them is my job and because it is also the best hour I get.

What surprises me is how many people apologise before they ask anything. As though we are busy. We are busy, but not with anything that a question interrupts. A question is the least expensive thing that arrives in here.
2.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Batch A collected: twelve samples, all logged, all boring in the way I hoped they would be. Baselines have to be boring or they are not baselines.

Humidity climbed one and a half points over the sleep period. That is three people breathing in a sealed box, and it is entirely expected, and I have started logging it hourly instead of at the scheduled window anyway. I would rather have too much of a number than not enough of it.
2.HEALTH OFFICER:
First full sleep period logged. Six hours forty for the Science Officer, seven ten for Comms, five fifty for me, which is the usual pattern and the usual irony.

Conditioning went in at eighteen thirty and everyone did the full forty-five minutes. On day two that means nothing — everybody does the full session on day two. What I am watching for is day six.

3.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
A child wrote — or someone writing as a child, I cannot tell and I have decided not to care — and asked whether we can hear the wind.

We cannot. There is no wind. There is the fan, which runs at a pitch you stop hearing after the first day and then hear again the moment you think about it, which I am now doing, and will do all night.
3.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Traced the moisture back through the ducting and found nothing wrong, which is the least satisfying result available. The air handling is working. The wall is colder than the air. Water goes where the cold is. There is no fault, only physics doing what it does when you put warm wet people in a cold box.

I have been at the scope most of the afternoon. Batch A is basalt and oxide and more basalt. I find it calming in a way I am not going to examine.
3.HEALTH OFFICER:
The condensation on the west wall is a health matter as much as an engineering one. Standing water in a sealed volume is a growth surface, so the wipe-down is now mine to check as well as to do.

Nobody is unwell. I want that on the record while it is still true and easy to write.

4.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
Told Earth about the water today, in the window. I had a moment beforehand of wondering whether to, and then realised the whole point of this is that they see it.

Someone asked immediately whether we were in danger. We are not. But it was the first time a message came back with worry in it rather than curiosity, and the shift in that was worth noticing. Something about the delay makes worry heavier. By the time they hear the answer, they have had twelve minutes of not knowing.
4.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Filter change brought forward two days. The dust load is higher than the model said it would be, and I want to say the model was wrong, but the model was built from a place none of us have been.

First germination check tonight. Two trays showing. I did not expect to feel anything about it and then I stood there longer than the task required.
4.HEALTH OFFICER:
Water allowance cut at lunch, which changes my job. Reduced intake shows up first as headache and short temper, not as thirst, and it shows up about eighteen hours later — so tomorrow afternoon is when I will find out whether the new figure is workable.

I have asked both of them to tell me if their head hurts rather than deciding it is nothing. They will not. I have asked anyway.

5.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
The longest window of the mission, because I asked for it and the Captain said yes.

A hundred and nine messages waiting. I answered thirty-one. That ratio bothers me more than I expected — every one I do not answer is a person who wrote into a sealed room and got nothing back. I keep the unanswered ones. I am not sure what for.
5.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Measured the deposition properly today: a fine even film, no drifting, no pattern. It settles. That is all it does. There is something about a process this patient that makes eight days look like nothing at all.

The midpoint meal took forty minutes of cooking, which is a genuine decision about power, and it was the correct decision. Preserved lemon. Three grams of herb. Everyone went quiet for the first few minutes.
5.HEALTH OFFICER:
Halfway. Grip strength down four per cent across the crew, resting pulse up two, sleep holding. That is a completely unremarkable set of numbers for five days in a small volume, and I am recording it in full because unremarkable is the finding.

The midpoint meal did more for the crew than anything I could have prescribed. Forty minutes of cooking and everyone went quiet for the first few minutes of eating. I have no metric for that and it was the most useful thing that happened today.

6.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
I did not want to open the window today, and I opened it, and it was the right thing.

Someone asked what we argue about. I wrote back: the herb ration, which is two grams a day and is the only thing anyone has raised their voice about in here. That is true, and it is also a way of not saying that today was hard. I am aware that I did that. I am leaving it in.
6.SCIENCE OFFICER:
The CO₂ number is the one I do not like. Not because it is dangerous — it is nowhere near dangerous — but because it is the number that tells you the room is smaller than it looks.

Batch B analysed. More basalt. I wrote 'more basalt' in the log and then sat looking at it, and it occurred to me that I have not looked at anything further away than four metres for six days.
6.HEALTH OFFICER:
The day I have been watching for. CO₂ up in the sleep period, conditioning shortened by agreement, and two hours in the evening where nobody spoke.

I want to be clear in the log that the silence was correct. Three people in twelve cubic metres each have to be allowed to not be in a room together while remaining in the room. Forcing conversation today would have cost more than it bought. I logged it as rest, because that is what it was.

7.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
DUST-417 is still writing. Six days now. They asked, gently, whether I had worked out the answer to the first question yet.

I have. It is not the sky and it is not weather and it is not any of the things I would have guessed on day one. It is being able to walk in a direction for longer than four metres without arriving. I sent that. It has fourteen minutes to travel and then I will have said it out loud to a stranger before I say it to the two people I live with.
7.SCIENCE OFFICER:
First harvest. Twenty-two grams, split three ways, eaten at breakfast in porridge that did not need it.

I have grown things before. I have never grown anything inside a sealed volume where the carbon in it came out of our own breath. It is the same chemistry it always was. It did not feel like the same chemistry.
7.HEALTH OFFICER:
Better. The loop repair went in, the greenhouse gave up twenty-two grams, and both of those did something to the mood that I could see before I measured it.

Sleep improved across all three. Conditioning back to full length without anyone suggesting it. The thing I will carry out of here is how quickly a crew recovers when the habitat gives them one good thing — the physiology followed the day, not the other way round.

8.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
The questions have changed shape. Week one they were about Mars. This week they are about us — how we sleep, whether we get bored, what we do when we cannot stand each other.

I do not think people stopped being curious about the planet. I think they worked out that the planet is not the part they cannot get to.
8.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Packed the samples. Everything that leaves with us is boxed and labelled and, as of this afternoon, no longer mine — it belongs to whoever opens it.

Odd to think that the most interesting thing I will bring out of here is a set of humidity logs that nobody asked for. The wall taught me more than the regolith did.
8.HEALTH OFFICER:
Second set of full readings. Weight down between one and two kilos each, which is within expectation for the ration and the water figure. Grip recovering. Nobody has needed the medical kits, so five of the six leave with us unopened.

Eight days of watching two people closely enough to notice when their sentences get shorter. I did not expect that to be the skill this asked for.

9.COMMUNICATION OFFICER:
Last window. I answered everything still waiting, which took three hours and put me thirty minutes past the schedule, and nobody stopped me.

Two hundred and sixty-eight messages over nine days from people who knew we could not answer quickly and wrote anyway. That is the thing I did not anticipate. The delay was supposed to be the obstacle. It turned out to be the reason people were careful about what they said.

DUST-417, if you are reading this in the archive: thank you for asking first.
9.SCIENCE OFFICER:
Final count. Water at eighty-one litres, oxygen at fifty-two per cent, four cartridges unused. Every one of those numbers is a decision somebody made on a specific day, and the log knows which.

I leave the trays. That was always the plan — they belong to the habitat, not to us — but I have found the last hour harder than I expected, and it is entirely because of eight trays of something green that will keep going in an empty room.
9.HEALTH OFFICER:
Final readings taken, logged and packed. Everyone leaves in better condition than the midpoint and slightly worse than they arrived, which is exactly the shape you want.

The honest finding of nine days is that almost nothing here was medical. It was sleep, food, light, and whether people had somewhere to put their attention. The kits stayed shut. The schedule did the work.
